at.step: Merging: sort the intervals by start, then walk them once. Extend the current merged interval when the next one starts before it ends; otherwise start a new one. Everything left of the sweep is already final.

Inserting one new interval into an already-merged list finds the first interval ending after the new one starts, absorbs every interval it overlaps, and splices the result: a linear scan costs O(n); finding the place by binary search costs O(log n + r), but the shifting itself is still O(n).
Apache Flink’s session windows run exactly this merge: every arriving record starts its own window, and windows merge together whenever they sit closer than the configured gap.

syllabus.clause: earliest-finish-time greedy for maximum non-overlapping intervals

at.step: Consider bookings in some order, keeping each one that is still compatible with the ones already kept. Which rule always keeps the most bookings?
Earliest-start-time-first keeps three of the ten bookings: the long early booking it takes first blocks four shorter ones that would otherwise fit.
Shortest-booking-first keeps four of the ten: a short booking can still sit exactly where it blocks two longer, more useful ones.

Earliest-finish-time-first keeps five of the ten, the most of any rule tried. A smaller, separate eight-booking set traps a fourth rule, fewest-conflicts-first, at three kept against earliest-finish’s four.

The proof: take any optimal schedule and swap its first booking for the earliest-finishing one. It finishes no later, so nothing after it can newly collide; repeat down the rest by induction and the greedy set is reached without ever losing a booking.

syllabus.clause: minimum rooms via a min-heap of end times

at.step: How many rooms do the ten bookings need at minimum, so that no two bookings in the same room overlap?

Sort bookings by start; keep a min-heap of the end times of rooms in use. Reuse the room whose booking has already ended; otherwise open a new one. The heap’s final size, three, equals the depth — the busiest moment’s own booking count — because opening a room only ever happens when every open room is still genuinely busy.

The same answer comes from a simpler walk: turn every start into +1 and every end into −1, sort the endpoints, and track the running total’s peak. Same three, reached without a heap at all — a method with a name, coming next.
Does earliest-finish-time-first still win once every booking carries a weight, not just a slot to fill?

The earliest-finish greedy set is still worth only twenty-eight. The table OPT of j, equal to the larger of OPT of j minus one and the weight of j plus OPT of p of j, fills left to right over the finish-sorted bookings and reaches twenty-nine — a different, larger-value set, with p of j found by binary search.
